metadata.title: Hyperscaler dominance could goeth before a fall

content.text:
Giant tech companies seem to control the commanding heights of the emerging AI economy at this stage of the AI trade.
Why it matters: Owning the hyperscalers has been one of the most popular positions on Wall Street, but some argue they actually may be more vulnerable than they look.
The big picture: They've got all the money they need, via cash from their massively profitable business models and relatively cheap debt.
-
Hyperscalers are also in a prime strategic spot, as they can sell wholesale computing power and AI services, as well as consumer and enterprise applications like Meta's Muse or Alphabet's Gemini Tasks.
Reality check: If this whole AI thing goes down in a flaming crash, hyperscalers will essentially be fine. They'll write down a few hundred billion in investment losses and go back to their pastime of minting money and plowing it into share buybacks.
-
Plus, if things do get ugly, people are going to want to own giant blue chips with durable cash flows and fat profit margins. You know, Microsoft, Alphabet, Apple. Big Tech.
-
(And then there's the situation in which hyperscalers control giant slugs of stock in companies like Anthropic, which could mitigate potential competitive threats.)
Zoom out: For all those reasons, sometimes it does seem like the strongest Big Tech companies really can't lose.
Yes, but: Not everybody agrees.
-
"I think the most underappreciated risk when it comes to AI is the disruption risk to the big tech incumbents," Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, head of global equities at UBS Global Wealth Management, told Axios Tuesday, at a UBS event to discuss its 2027 outlook.
What they're saying: She said she is telling clients that market bounces could be opportunities "to balance exposure and to balance and diversify away from the largest index weights."
The bottom line: It was an interesting view. And it seemed consistent with wrinkles we noticed in the recent crop of earnings, which included surprising weakness in the core businesses of giants like Alphabet and Amazon, for example.
